comments.text:
17:46  (LTV is why)... guessing, but banks are also in the business of making money.  They currently have a contract for 80k at 12%.  On a 6yr they'd make 32k in interest.  They aren't just going to write that off.  (If they got the 80 today, they'd loan some out at a higher rate)

To get a 1k payment on a 6yr at 16% (since he reneged on 12% and is now a greater risk), given 22k rolled over, that's only a 24k vehicle (minus fees, commissions, etc, call it 16-18), and the bank only gets 25k interest.  But that's a 46k loan on an 18k vehicle so the loan-to-value (LTV) is 255%!  (Versus 138 on the 80k/58k).  No bank is signing that. 

To get LTV back to 140% means a total loan of 98k (70k value), because you're stuck paying fees and dealer etc.  IE 12k more value in the vehicle.  And that payment will never get down to 1k.

In 1970 I bought my first car, a 1963 Pontiac Tempest, for $400 cash - I saved for it. I can’t remember how many miles it had, but my father went with me to buy it, and included it on his auto insurance. I had just learned to drive and needed it for college where there was no reliable public transport. I had an embarrassing accident at low speed in a small city. I paid cash to repair it so I wouldn’t have to tell my parents or the insurance company for $500 cash - no cards for students back then! I worked part time and saved my money. I know the costs are MUCH higher now, so it’s even more important for first time car buyers without much money to buy an old used car and save money for any repairs that insurance doesn’t cover. You’re YOUNG - that’s what young people DO!!
P.S. I’m driving a 2009 Lexus sedan that I bought privately for $12,000 cash in 2014. It had 25,000 miles on it and has been pretty reliable. I hope it’s the last car I have to buy - I’m 75!
